prompt.context: A marketing vice-president of a major pharmaceutical firm is working on a business plan for a new revolutionary product. The researchers have developed eye drops which completely eliminate near sightedness in 60% of the cases (the cases caused by eye strain rather than irregularly shaped eye lenses) if the drops are used twice a day.
prompt.question:
Part I: The client needs a directional estimate of the retail price they should set for the drops so that he can complete the business plan. How would you help the client structure his thinking on the price, and what is your back-of-the-envelope estimate on the price that he should use in the business plan?

Part II: After agreeing on a price of approximately $200 per year, the client now wants a ballpark estimate of the U.S. market size. Specifically, what dollar level of sales might he be able to expect per year in the long run in the U.S. market?

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of nearsightedness cases are caused by eye strain vs. irregularly shaped lenses?
clarifying_info.a: 60% of nearsighted cases are caused by eye strain and would be helped by the drops.

clarifying_info.q: Is the product a one-time cure or an ongoing treatment?
clarifying_info.a: It is an ongoing treatment; drops must be used twice a day to maintain the effect.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current competitive landscape for corrective eyewear?
clarifying_info.a: The main alternatives are eyeglasses and contact lenses.

framework: Pricing: Determine value relative to alternatives (eyeglasses, contact lenses) — use value-based pricing
Pricing: Consider the full cost to the consumer of the best substitute, including accessories, optometrist fees, and time/convenience
Pricing: Note that the new product may command a premium due to superior convenience and efficacy (no handling, no cleaning)
Pricing: Advanced considerations include dynamic pricing strategy (start high, reduce over time to understand elasticity) and pricing where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
Market sizing: Estimate U.S. population, segment by corrective-eyewear users, nearsighted share, product-eligible share, and adoption rate
Market sizing: Multiply addressable users by annual price to get revenue estimate

questions.prompt: Part I: How would you estimate a retail price for the eye drops?
questions.guidance: A strong answer structures pricing in tiers of sophistication. First tier (basic): benchmark against direct substitutes — eyeglasses cost ~$120 and last 2 years, so a 2-year supply could be priced at $120 (~$60/year). Second tier (intermediate): sum the full annual cost of the most expensive substitute. Contact lenses: $120/pair + ~$60 for one lost lens = $180; optometrist fees ~$100/year; cleaning supplies ~$25/year; total ~$305/year, so drops could be priced at ~$305. Third tier (advanced): premium pricing above substitutes justified by superior convenience and efficacy; dynamic pricing to test elasticity; MR=MC analysis. The case accepts ~$200/year as the agreed working price.

math.setup: Full annual cost of contact lens alternative
steps: Contact lenses: $120 per pair + $60 replacement for one lost lens = $180/year
math.answer: $305/year (upper bound); ~$60/year (lower bound using eyeglasses); agreed working price $200/year

questions.prompt: Part II: Estimate the long-run annual U.S. sales for the eye drops.
questions.guidance: A strong answer walks through a structured market sizing funnel: U.S. population → share using corrective eyewear → share that is nearsighted → share the product helps (given by client) → adoption rate → multiply by price. Each assumption should be stated explicitly and be directionally reasonable.

math.setup: Funnel: U.S. population × % corrective eyewear users × % nearsighted × % helped by drops × adoption rate × price per year
steps: % of those who are nearsighted: 70% → 50M × 0.70 = 35 million
Adoption rate estimate: 40–60%, use midpoint 50% → 21M × 0.50 = 10.5 million users
math.answer: ~$2.1 billion per year in long-run U.S. sales

recommendation: Set the retail price at approximately $200 per year — above the cost of eyeglasses but below the full annual cost of contact lenses, reflecting the product's superior convenience and efficacy
Estimated long-run U.S. annual sales are approximately $2.1 billion, based on ~10.5 million addressable adopters at $200/year
risks: Adoption rate could be lower than 50% if consumers are skeptical of a new drug or prefer established alternatives
Price sensitivity: at $200/year, the product is 3x the annualized cost of eyeglasses; positioning and education will be critical
The 60% efficacy rate means 40% of nearsighted customers receive no benefit, creating potential reputational risk
Regulatory and reimbursement hurdles could delay market entry or suppress addressable market
next_steps: Conduct primary market research to validate willingness-to-pay and adoption assumptions
Analyze insurance reimbursement landscape to determine net out-of-pocket cost for consumers
Develop a phased pricing strategy (launch high, with potential reductions as elasticity data accumulates)
Build sensitivity analysis around adoption rate (40%–60%) and price ($150–$305) for the business plan
